transcript.content: Hello, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

Well, I guess the main thing is I keep forgetting things I really shouldn’t be forgetting. It’s not just little things like where I put my glasses—though I do that too sometimes—it’s more important stuff. Like I’ll have a heart follow-up appointment and somehow it just slips past me, or the clinic calls and I’m supposed to call them back and I don’t do it, not because I don’t care, but because it just… disappears from my head.

And then there are practical things too. I’ll go to do a repair job, something I know how to do, and I’ll show up without the right tools. Then I’m standing there feeling foolish because I had every intention of bringing them. It’s frustrating, and honestly kind of embarrassing at my age. That’s really what brought me in.
Have you been feeling down or depressed lately?

I don’t know that I’d call it depressed, exactly. I mean, I get frustrated with myself, sure—especially when I mess something up or forget something important—and sometimes that can sit with me for a while. But “down” like a heavy sadness all the time? I’m not sure that’s really what’s going on.

I guess I’d say I’ve been more annoyed and embarrassed than depressed. But maybe I’m not the best judge of it. What do you mean by depressed—like not wanting to do anything, or just feeling low?
Because of your memory problems, do you need help managing your daily responsibilities?

I’m still mostly handling things myself day to day, but… yes, in some ways it’s gotten to the point where people have to sort of keep after me.

Like with the senior-center repair group, I used to be someone they could count on. If I said I’d show up or bring something, that was that. And now there’ve been enough times where I’ve forgotten or not followed through right that I can tell they don’t rely on me the same way. That bothers me a lot, because I don’t want to be the guy who makes extra work for everyone.

And with my heart follow-ups, the doctor’s office has had to call and chase me down because I missed appointments or didn’t get back to them. They’re polite about it, but it’s embarrassing. So I wouldn’t say someone is managing my whole life for me, but I do seem to need more reminders and nudging than I used to, especially for things that actually matter.
Because of your memory problems, have you had to stop managing your own finances?

No, I don’t think I’ve had to stop managing them. I mean, I still handle my own money, bills, that sort of thing. At least, I haven’t turned it over to anybody else or anything like that.

Now, I do try to be careful, because finances are one of those things where a small mistake can turn into a bigger headache pretty fast. But I wouldn’t say I’ve stopped managing them. If anything, I just… I may double-check myself more, or feel like I should. But no, I’m still doing it myself.
Has a doctor told you that you have a medical condition affecting your brain or nervous system that could be causing these memory problems?

No, not that I know of. I mean, no doctor has sat me down and said, “You have this brain or nerve condition and that’s why your memory is acting up,” or anything like that.

I’ve had doctors bring up the memory issue in a general way, and they ask questions like you’re asking, but as far as I understand it, nobody has given me a specific explanation like that. Unless there’s something in my chart I’m not remembering or didn’t understand right, but I don’t think so.
Do you ever get confused about what day it is or where you are?

Not really… I mean, I don’t think I get confused about where I am. I know I’m at home, or at the doctor’s office, or wherever I’m supposed to be. I’m not finding myself somewhere and thinking, “How did I get here?” or anything like that.

The day thing… I may have to think for a second sometimes, like, “Is it Tuesday or Wednesday?” especially if the week’s been kind of the same every day, but I don’t know if I’d call that being confused. I usually can figure it out by looking at my phone or remembering what I had scheduled. So, no, I haven’t noticed any real trouble with that, at least not in the way I think you mean.
Has any doctor ever told you that you’ve had a stroke?

No, I don’t believe so. Nobody has ever told me, “You had a stroke,” at least not that I remember.

I mean, that’s the kind of thing I think would stick with me, or my family would be bringing it up, or it would have been explained pretty clearly. I’ve had doctors ask about it on forms or during visits, like checking boxes and all that, but I haven’t been told that I had one. So as far as I know, no.
Have you ever been told you have Parkinson’s disease?

No, not that I know of. I’ve never had a doctor tell me I have Parkinson’s disease.

I mean, I’ve heard of it, of course, and I think if somebody had said that to me directly, I’d remember it, or at least I’d hope I would. Doctors ask about all kinds of things on those forms, and sometimes it all runs together, but as far as I understand my own medical history, nobody has diagnosed me with Parkinson’s.
Have your memory problems caused you to miss paying any bills?

I don’t think it’s been bills so much, no—or at least that’s not the main thing I’ve noticed. I usually have some kind of routine with those, or I’ll see the envelope sitting there and it reminds me.

What’s really been bothering me is I keep forgetting things I feel like I really shouldn’t be forgetting. Like I’ve missed or nearly missed heart follow-up appointments, or I’ll forget I was supposed to call the clinic back, and then later I’ll think, “Oh, come on, I was supposed to do that yesterday.” And with repair stuff, I’ve shown up without the right tools, which is embarrassing because then it’s like I made the trip and can’t even do what I came to do.

So, bills specifically, I don’t know that I’d say that’s been the big problem. It’s more those day-to-day responsibilities and appointments where I’m dropping the ball.
Have you had trouble finding the right words when you’re speaking?

Not really, no—at least not in any way that’s stood out to me. I mean, everybody has those moments where a word is on the tip of your tongue and you say, “What’s that thing called?” but I don’t think I’m having that more than other people my age.

I can usually say what I mean. Sometimes I might pause or talk around something for a second, but I wouldn’t say I’m sitting there unable to find words or having people finish my sentences for me all the time. So, no, I haven’t really noticed that as a problem.
Because of your memory problems, have you had to stop driving?

No, I haven’t had to stop driving because of memory problems. I still drive.

I mean, I try to be sensible about it—I’m not saying I’m perfect or anything—but I haven’t gotten to the point where someone told me I shouldn’t drive, and I haven’t decided I need to give it up. If I’m going somewhere unfamiliar, I might double-check where I’m going or think through the route ahead of time, but I haven’t stopped driving because of memory.
Have you ever been told you have a brain injury?

No, I don’t believe so. Nobody’s ever sat me down and said, “You have a brain injury,” at least not that I remember.

I mean, I’ve had bumps and knocks like most people do over a lifetime, but if you’re asking whether a doctor ever diagnosed me with a brain injury, or told me that was the explanation for anything, then no—not that I know of.
Because of your memory problems, do you need help with basic self-care like bathing or dressing?

No, not for things like that. I can bathe myself and get dressed on my own.

I might take my time sometimes, or have to think for a second about what I was about to do, but I don’t need someone coming in and helping me wash or put my clothes on. That would be a different level, I think, and I’m not there. Basic stuff like showering, shaving, getting dressed—I handle that myself.
Have you ever been told you have Alzheimer’s disease or dementia?

No, I don’t think anyone has told me that. I mean, if a doctor had said the words “Alzheimer’s” or “dementia” to me as something I have, I feel like I would remember that, because that’s a pretty big thing to hear.

People can say things casually sometimes, you know, like “Oh, everybody forgets things as they get older,” or they ask questions about memory, but as far as an actual diagnosis—no, not that I know of. Nobody has sat me down and said I have Alzheimer’s disease or dementia.
Because of your memory problems, have you had to stop taking your medications on your own?

No, I wouldn’t say I’ve had to stop taking my medications on my own. That hasn’t really been the issue, at least not the way you’re asking it.

The bigger thing—the thing that’s been bothering me and kind of embarrassing me—is I keep forgetting things I really should be keeping track of. Like heart follow-up appointments, or needing to call the clinic back when they leave a message, and then I’ll remember later and think, “Why didn’t I just do that?” Or I’ll be getting ready for something, like a repair job, and I show up without the right tools, even though I know better. That kind of thing makes me feel like I’m dropping the ball.

But actually stopping my medicines because of memory problems, no, I don’t think that’s happened.
Has anyone close to you told you they’ve noticed your memory getting worse?

Yeah, people close to me have noticed, mostly because it’s the kind of stuff that affects the day-to-day. They’ll say, “Did you call the clinic back?” or “Weren’t you supposed to have that heart follow-up?” and then I realize I either forgot completely or I meant to do it and it just slipped away from me.

And it’s not just appointments. If I’m doing something practical, like a repair job, I’ll get there and then realize I didn’t bring the right tools, which is frustrating because I know better than that. That’s the sort of thing that’s been bringing me in, really. It feels like I keep forgetting things I shouldn’t be forgetting, and other people have started pointing it out too.
Have you ever been told you have any disease or condition affecting your brain?

Not that I know of, no. I mean, nobody has told me, “You have a brain disease” or anything like that.

I guess I’m not totally sure what all would count under that—like if you mean a stroke, tumor, seizures, or some kind of memory disease, I haven’t been told I have anything like that. At least no doctor has sat me down and explained it that way to me. If something like that had been said plainly, I think it would’ve stuck with me.
Because of your memory problems, have you had to stop doing any regular activities you used to handle on your own?

Yeah… I mean, not completely stop everything, like I’m not helpless or anything, but there are definitely things I used to handle on my own that people don’t really trust me with the same way now.

The senior-center repair group is a big one. I used to be one of the guys they could count on to show up and have what was needed, know what I was there for, that sort of thing. Lately it’s more like… they can’t rely on me the way they used to, because I’ll forget something important or not have followed through the way I meant to. That bothers me a lot, honestly, because I liked being useful there.

And with my heart follow-ups, the doctor’s office has had to chase me down more than once because I missed things or didn’t get back to them. I don’t like that either. I used to be able to keep that kind of thing straight better, and now it feels like other people have to keep after me. So, yes, it has affected regular things I used to manage myself, even if I’m not totally stopped from doing them.
Has any doctor ever told you that your memory problems are being caused by another medical condition?

No, not that I can remember. Nobody’s told me, “Your memory trouble is because of this other medical problem,” at least not in a clear way like that.

I’ve had doctors talk to me about follow-ups and things I’m supposed to keep track of, but I don’t think anyone has said there’s some specific condition causing the memory problems. If they did, either I didn’t understand it that way or it didn’t stick, but as far as I know, no.
Have you ever had any brain imaging, like a CT scan or MRI of your head?

I’m not really sure. I don’t remember having an MRI or CT scan of my head, at least not one that stands out to me.

I mean, I’ve had medical appointments and tests over the years, and sometimes they put you in machines or send you for things and you just kind of do what they tell you, so I don’t want to swear absolutely that I never had one. But if someone had told me, “We’re scanning your brain,” I feel like I’d remember that, because that sounds like a big deal.

So… as far as I know, no, I haven’t had brain imaging. Or if I did, nobody explained it to me in a way that stuck.

They’ll say, “Did you call the clinic back?” or “Weren’t you supposed to have that heart follow-up?” and then I realize I either forgot completely or I meant to do it and it just slipped away from me.

And it’s not just appointments. If I’m doing something practical, like a repair job, I’ll get there and then realize I didn’t bring the right tools, which is frustrating because I know better than that. That’s the sort of thing that’s been bringing me in, really. It feels like I keep forgetting things I shouldn’t be forgetting, and other people have started pointing it out too.

doctor.intent: Determine whether there is a documented general medical condition causing the cognitive symptoms, which would distinguish mild neurocognitive disorder due to a known physiological condition (F06.7) from unspecified neurocognitive disorder/dementia (F09/F03).
doctor.question: Have you ever been told you have any disease or condition affecting your brain?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about whether I have been diagnosed with a brain disease or neurological condition, which is not covered by the ADHD symptom profile items listed.

patient.answer:
Not that I know of, no. I mean, nobody has told me, “You have a brain disease” or anything like that.

I guess I’m not totally sure what all would count under that—like if you mean a stroke, tumor, seizures, or some kind of memory disease, I haven’t been told I have anything like that. At least no doctor has sat me down and explained it that way to me. If something like that had been said plainly, I think it would’ve stuck with me.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the memory decline has impaired instrumental daily functioning enough to support major neurocognitive disorder rather than mild neurocognitive disorder or unspecified cognitive disorder.
doctor.question: Because of your memory problems, have you had to stop doing any regular activities you used to handle on your own?

target_item.name: Functional Impairment
target_item.manifestation: It’s gotten to where the senior-center repair group can’t count on me the way they used to, and my doctor’s office has had to chase me about missed heart follow-ups.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether the memory problems have caused loss of independence or stopping regular activities, which is most directly about functional impairment from the symptoms.

patient.answer:
Yeah… I mean, not completely stop everything, like I’m not helpless or anything, but there are definitely things I used to handle on my own that people don’t really trust me with the same way now.

The senior-center repair group is a big one. I used to be one of the guys they could count on to show up and have what was needed, know what I was there for, that sort of thing. Lately it’s more like… they can’t rely on me the way they used to, because I’ll forget something important or not have followed through the way I meant to. That bothers me a lot, honestly, because I liked being useful there.

And with my heart follow-ups, the doctor’s office has had to chase me down more than once because I missed things or didn’t get back to them. I don’t like that either. I used to be able to keep that kind of thing straight better, and now it feels like other people have to keep after me. So, yes, it has affected regular things I used to manage myself, even if I’m not totally stopped from doing them.

doctor.intent: Determine whether there is documented evidence of another medical condition causing the cognitive decline, which would distinguish major neurocognitive disorder due to another medical condition (F06.7) from unspecified dementia/neurocognitive disorder (F03/F09).
doctor.question: Has any doctor ever told you that your memory problems are being caused by another medical condition?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether another medical condition has been identified as the cause of the memory problems, which is about medical etiology/exclusion rather than any listed ADHD symptom or requirement.

patient.answer:
No, not that I can remember. Nobody’s told me, “Your memory trouble is because of this other medical problem,” at least not in a clear way like that.

I’ve had doctors talk to me about follow-ups and things I’m supposed to keep track of, but I don’t think anyone has said there’s some specific condition causing the memory problems. If they did, either I didn’t understand it that way or it didn’t stick, but as far as I know, no.

doctor.intent: Determine whether there is a documented medical cause for the cognitive decline, which would distinguish mild neurocognitive disorder due to another medical condition (F06.7) from unspecified dementia or unspecified mental disorder due to known physiological condition.
doctor.question: Have you ever had any brain imaging, like a CT scan or MRI of your head?

target_item.reason: The question asks about prior brain imaging such as CT or MRI of the head, which is not covered by any listed ADHD symptom profile or requirement.

patient.answer:
I’m not really sure. I don’t remember having an MRI or CT scan of my head, at least not one that stands out to me.

I mean, I’ve had medical appointments and tests over the years, and sometimes they put you in machines or send you for things and you just kind of do what they tell you, so I don’t want to swear absolutely that I never had one. But if someone had told me, “We’re scanning your brain,” I feel like I’d remember that, because that sounds like a big deal.

So… as far as I know, no, I haven’t had brain imaging. Or if I did, nobody explained it to me in a way that stuck.

No specific brain disease or other medical/neurologic condition has been identified in the interview, arguing against mild cognitive disorder due to known physiological condition (F06.7). Functional decline beyond a purely subjective complaint makes an unspecified organic/mental disorder (F09) less fitting than unspecified dementia.
